newsitem.title: USA: Glickman to call EU, says meat deal still possible.
newsitem.headline: Glickman to call EU, says meat deal still possible.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said he would try to call his EU counterpart later on Tuesday in hopes of reaching a meat trade pact and averting a transatlantic disruption this week.
"I'll get on the phone with EU commissioner (Franz) Fischler," Glickman said.
"We are within striking distance" of a pact, he said, but it was even odds whether the two sides would agree or not.

At issue in the so-called veterinary equivalency talks was whether the two sides, which use different meat inspection regimes, could agree on a method for determining that each other's products were safe.

Since April 1, new EU regulations have cut off shipments of U.S. poultry worth $50 million a year. The United States has said it would remove more than 100 European meat and poultry plants from its approved list, which would halt meat sales, mostly Danish pork, to U.S. buyers worth $300 million.
"This Thursday is the end of the line," Glickman said in a breakfast-time appearance before farm broadcasters.
Glickman told reporters afterward that the call to Fischler had not been arranged yet but he believed both wanted to speak to the other.
Paul Drazek, Glickman's trade adviser, said he unsuccessfully tried telephoning EU officials earlier in the day.

The agriculture secretary told the broadcasters that two so-far intractable issues remained -- EU desire for retroactive "regionalization" on the U.S. part and U.S. desire for EU acceptance of its methods of decontamination of poultry meat, which he described as superior to EU practices.

Each request would require significant accomodation by the other side. Retroactive regionalization could be achieved only by the lengthy U.S. rulemaking process, Glickman said, and EU codes would need similar changes on the poultry issue.
Negotiations were "at their critical stage right now," Glickman told the broadcasters.
In response to a question from the audience, Glickman said the outcome of the meat talks would have no bearing on the long-running dispute over synthetic growth hormones in cattle.
"Right now, no, I do not expect a 'deal' on beef hormones," he said, adding a WTO ruling was expected soon.
